stablecoins.title: Visa Launches Stablecoin Platform for Banks and Fintechs | Phoebe Duong posted on the topic | LinkedIn
stablecoins.desc:
Visa just launched a platform for banks and fintechs to run stablecoins. Not a new stablecoin. A system to run the ones that already exist. 𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗶𝘁 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀: Visa already runs $4.5B a year in stablecoin settlement. And Visa isn’t alone here. Banks, payment companies, and asset managers are all racing toward the same thing: stablecoins. 𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐞𝐬 𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐞𝐚𝐭𝐡 ↳ Mint, redeem, and move stablecoins from one place, not five different vendors ↳ Connect bank accounts with approvals already built in ↳ Use Visa’s wallets, or plug in the ones already have ↳ Keep the same treasury and settlement process. Stablecoins just run quietly underneath The platform’s first supported asset is Open USD. Open USD is the one to watch. Open Standard built it, the same group backing Visa. It shares its yield with the banks and fintechs that use it. USDC works differently. There, the yield mostly stays with Circle. For years the question was: should banks touch stablecoins. Now it’s: whose rails do they touch them on. Visa doesn’t need to win the stablecoin race. It just needs banks to run every stablecoin through Visa. Here’s the real question: as more companies build this same layer, do banks end up with more choice? Or do they get stuck with whoever moves first?
---------------------------- I’m 𝗣𝗵𝗼𝗲𝗯𝗲 𝗗𝘂𝗼𝗻𝗴, GTM and Adoption Strategist focused on crypto and stablecoin products in APAC. 𝗙𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗼𝘄 for more on tokenization, stablecoin infrastructure, and digital asset adoption.

stablecoins.title: HSBC Issues Digitally Native Structured Note on Blockchain in Hong Kong | Phoebe Duong posted on the topic | LinkedIn
stablecoins.desc:
HSBC just issued its first digitally native structured note in Hong Kong. Not tokenized later. Built on blockchain from day one. 𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗶𝘁 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀: Structured products aren’t small in Asia. They drive 20 to 30 percent of revenue at many Asian wealth platforms. Regional volume tops $400 billion a year. Hong Kong is the biggest issuance hub. This pilot sits inside that market. Not a side experiment. 𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐞𝐬 𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐞𝐚𝐭𝐡 ↳ Issuance moves from paper to native token creation ↳ Settlement and servicing sit on one shared ledger ↳ No more separate reconciliation across issuer, paying agent, distributor ↳ Investor experience looks the same. Infrastructure underneath does not This builds on HSBC’s wider digital asset push. Orion for tokenized bonds. A retail gold token in Hong Kong. Marketnode ran this deal as tokenisation agent and digital paying agent. It’s backed by Euroclear , SGX Group , and Temasek . HSBC hasn’t shared deal size, tenor, or the underlying asset. This is a pilot, not a template yet. This is not proof tokenization has arrived. It’s proof where institutions are heading. Today, a private placement. Tomorrow, bonds, funds, and other real world assets could follow. The real question: will onchain infrastructure stay invisible, or will investors start expecting it as something they can see and choose.
---------------------------- I’m Phoebe Duong, GTM and Adoption Strategist focused on crypto and stablecoin products in APAC. 𝗙𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗼𝘄 for more on tokenization, stablecoin infrastructure, and digital asset adoption.

stablecoins.title: 𝗧𝗼𝗽 𝟮𝟬 𝗜𝗻𝗳𝗿𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗣𝗹𝗮𝘆𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗣𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗶𝗻 𝗣𝗮𝘆𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝗶𝗻 𝗔𝗣𝗔𝗖 💾 Stablecoins in APAC stopped being a regulatory question. They became… | Phoebe Duong
stablecoins.desc:
𝗧𝗼𝗽 𝟮𝟬 𝗜𝗻𝗳𝗿𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗣𝗹𝗮𝘆𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗣𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗶𝗻 𝗣𝗮𝘆𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝗶𝗻 𝗔𝗣𝗔𝗖 💾 Stablecoins in APAC stopped being a regulatory question. They became an infrastructure question. 𝗦𝗶𝘅 𝗹𝗮𝘆𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗱𝗼𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸: • Issuers minting the stablecoins themselves: StraitsX , Circle , Paxos , Ripple • Custody and wallet infrastructure holding the keys: Fystack, Cobo , Fireblocks • Merchant gateways turning stablecoins into checkout: Triple-A , FOMO Pay , Alchemy Pay • B2B and treasury rails settling cross-border flows: Saber Money , Due , Conduit , TransFi • Card programs spending stablecoins like fiat: DCS Card Centre, RedotPay • Super-app and enterprise integrations making it invisible: Grab x StraitsX, OKX Pay
• Enterprise tooling embedding crypto into existing rails: Xendit , MetaComp Most of these names will never reach a consumer headline. That’s the point. A user in Jakarta paying with QRIS. A merchant in Singapore settling via SGQR. A supplier in Vietnam getting paid in minutes instead of days. None of them see a blockchain. They see a payment that just works. 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗶𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗮 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗶𝗻 𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘆. 𝗜𝘁’𝘀 𝗮𝗻 𝗶𝗻𝗳𝗿𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘆. And the players who win are the ones who make stablecoins disappear into the rails everyone already uses. -----------------------------
I’m Phoebe Duong - GTM & Adoption Strategist focused on crypto and stablecoin products in APAC. [𝗙𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗼𝘄] for more insights on Market Behavior, Compliance & Growth Infrastructure. [𝗥𝗲𝗽𝗼𝘀𝘁] if this added value 🤝

stablecoins.title: Stablecoins aren't just a tech shift, they're a coordination challenge | Phoebe Duong posted on the topic | LinkedIn
stablecoins.desc:
𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐬 𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐧’𝐭 𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭 𝐚 𝐭𝐞𝐜𝐡𝐧𝐨𝐥𝐨𝐠𝐲 𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐟𝐭 - 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐲’𝐫𝐞 𝐚 𝐜𝐨𝐨𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐞𝐧𝐠𝐞. For years, the conversation around stablecoins has focused on speed, cost, and real-time settlement.
And yes, those advantages are real.
But zoom out, and a more important layer emerges: ↳ Global payments don’t run on one system. They run on many jurisdictions. 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐨𝐟 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐢𝐧 𝐢𝐧𝐟𝐫𝐚:
A single transaction may be technically seamless…
• Wallet → wallet
• Instant settlement
• Full transparency But operationally?
• Compliance varies by region
• Licensing frameworks evolve at different speeds
• Risk models are not standardized
• Local regulators define the rules of engagement This isn’t friction. → This is the system adapting in real time. 𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐦𝐞𝐚𝐧𝐬:
Stablecoins don’t replace the existing financial system.
They interact with it.
• TradFi brings trust, regulation, and distribution
• Onchain brings programmability, speed, and efficiency → The future is not either side winning. → It’s interoperability becoming the default. 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐨𝐩𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐮𝐧𝐢𝐭𝐲:
As regions take different approaches - from strict regulation to innovation sandboxes - we’re seeing a global experiment unfold. • The US focuses on enforcement & protection
• The EU standardizes with frameworks like MiCA
• Asia balances innovation with regulatory clarity
• Emerging markets explore phased adoption Fragmentation today… → can become resilience tomorrow. 𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐢𝐬 𝐡𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠:
• Cross-border flows becoming near real-time
• Compliance embedded directly into payment rails
• Wallets evolving into regulated financial interfaces
• Treasury and FX moving closer to protocol-level We’re not just building faster payments.
We’re building globally-aware financial infrastructure. Stablecoins have global potential, but adoption is a local journey.
And that’s exactly what makes this space so interesting right now.
------------------------

stablecoins.title: Stablecoin Adoption in Asia Driven by Economic Necessity | Phoebe Duong posted on the topic | LinkedIn
stablecoins.desc:
One thing I’ve learned studying stablecoin adoption across Asia: People may all be using USDT or USDC,
but they are not using them for the same reasons. In places like #Vietnam, #Pakistan, and the #Philippines, stablecoins often function less like “crypto assets” and more like everyday financial infrastructure. A Filipino overseas worker sending money home.
A Pakistani freelancer trying to avoid currency devaluation.
A Vietnamese user holding USDT as savings instead of local currency. That behavior looks very different from markets like Singapore, Hong Kong, or Korea. In those markets, stablecoin activity is more institutional:
→ trading liquidity
→ treasury operations
→ cross-border settlement
→ programmable payments Meanwhile in parts of South and Southeast Asia, the behavior is much more necessity-driven. People are using stablecoins because:
→ remittances are expensive
→ local currencies are unstable
→ banking access is limited
→ global USD access matters That’s why I think Asia’s stablecoin story is often misunderstood. The biggest adoption drivers here are not narratives.
They’re economic pain points. And honestly, this is probably what makes Asia one of the most important regions to watch in crypto right now: People here are adopting stablecoins less because of crypto narratives -
and more because they offer practical solutions for cross-border payments, savings, and global dollar access. Curious how others see this trend evolving across different Asian markets 😊 ----------------------------------
